0: We want to predict a clothing category from a picture. A catalogue could use that prediction to help organise new items. This is supervised multiclass classification: our target is one of ten clothing labels. Logistic regression is our baseline. We compare it with a nearest-neighbour classifier and a CNN to see what the extra complexity buys us and which mistakes remain.
1: Fashion-MNIST gives us 70,000 labelled grayscale images in a common format. Its balance makes accuracy easy to interpret: each category has equal representation and we give each mistake equal cost. Accuracy is our primary metric. We also report macro-F1 and class recall because a good overall score can hide a weak category.
2: Each image has 784 unsigned eight-bit pixel values. The target is an integer category label. Our exploration found no missing values, invalid labels or exact duplicates in the development data. About half the training pixels are zero. We kept the observations and divided intensities by 255. That fixed transformation needs no fitted statistics. Logistic regression and kNN receive flattened pixels; the CNN receives the original grid in one channel.
3: The publisher supplied the 10,000-image test set. We split the remaining 60,000 into 48,000 training and 12,000 validation images. We took the first split from StratifiedGroupKFold. Stratification preserved class proportions, and grouping would have kept identical images together. Each category was exactly ten percent of every split, so resampling was unnecessary. We used one validation holdout for tuning. We fitted the models on training data, compared candidate settings on validation, and froze the checkpoints before scoring the test set once.
4: For kNN we tried three, five and nine neighbours. Three won on validation. Here two of the three nearest images are pullovers, so the coat is misclassified. To measure training accuracy, each image voted using only the three nearest other images. That gave 85.27 percent, close to 85.04 percent on test. Its test advantage over the logistic baseline was just 0.71 percentage points.
5: Logistic regression gives each pixel a weight for each class. Adding the weighted pixels and intercept gives a class score. The heatmap shows contributions to the predicted score. Of four L2 regularisation settings, C equal to 0.1 had the highest validation accuracy. Our baseline reached 87.42 percent on training and 84.33 percent on test. Its three-point gap is modest. A linear score also limits how this model can combine neighbouring pixels into patterns.
6: The CNN keeps the grid. The first convolution learns 32 local filters and the second learns 64. Pooling reduces the spatial dimensions, then a 128-unit dense layer combines the features. We used dropout of 0.25 and restored epoch 12. At that checkpoint accuracy was 95.67 percent on training and 91.79 percent on test. That is a 7.46-point gain over our baseline. The remaining train-to-test gap motivated a closer look at the learning curves.
7: For this coat, gradient saliency highlights pixels where a small change would most affect the Coat score. Occlusion asks what happens to the same score when we cover a patch. As the patch moves, the readout shows the change in the raw score. Both maps describe sensitivity for this image. Later we will use SHAP to measure signed contributions to a probability.
8: We chose settings on validation accuracy. Within each CNN run we restored the epoch with lowest validation loss. Across configurations, the wider CNN without weight decay won. The two wider versions were very close across three seeds, and weight decay had higher mean shirt recall. We retained the original accuracy-first choice. Those seeds measure training variation on the same split.
9: Training loss continued falling after epoch 12. Validation loss reached its minimum there, so later epochs improved training fit without improving that criterion. Training stopped at epoch 17 and restored epoch 12. That divergence is evidence of overfitting with further training.
10: The summary shows the size of the improvement. kNN gains less than one point over logistic regression. The CNN gains more than seven and also leads on macro-F1. It had already won on validation; final testing confirmed the choice. Which items does it still miss?
11: Each confusion-matrix row starts with a thousand actual items. Read across a row to see the predictions. The CNN recognises 99 percent of bags but only 67.6 percent of shirts. Equal class sizes make that difference particularly easy to interpret.
12: Of the thousand actual shirts, 324 were missed. Look at the first pair: 127 shirts were called T-shirt or top, while only 63 T-shirts or tops were called shirt. The same asymmetry appears for coats and pullovers. Similar outlines are a plausible explanation at this low resolution. The counts establish the direction of the errors; the images alone cannot establish their cause.
13: Both SHAP plots explain the CNN's Coat probability. On the left, each dot is one validation image. Its horizontal position shows how much that quadrant raised or lowered the probability. Colour gives its average brightness. Across these 100 images, upper right has the largest average absolute effect. On the right is one actual shirt predicted as Coat. Starting at the training-reference average of 14.0 percent, all four quadrants push toward Coat, reaching 58.3 percent. For this shirt, lower right contributes most, about 15.5 percentage points. The answer depends on our region boundaries and reference images.
14: We used one validation split, so repeated choices could adapt to those images. The CNN also differs from the other models in capacity and training, so the comparison cannot isolate the benefit of convolution alone. Fashion-MNIST contains small, standardised images. My next experiment would evaluate the frozen CNN on independently labelled phone photos with different lighting and backgrounds.
15: The CNN was the best of our three models on this benchmark. It improved test accuracy by 7.46 points over logistic regression. But if a catalogue particularly needs reliable shirt labels, overall accuracy hides a practical weakness: the CNN misses about a third of actual shirts. That is the result I would investigate before relying on it for new photographs. Thank you. What questions do you have?
16: Fit the classifiers. Divide raw pixel intensities by the known maximum of 255; this uses no estimated statistics. Choose C, k, CNN settings and checkpoint. All models use identical source indices. Only the first split from StratifiedGroupKFold was used. Freeze all three checkpoints, verify their hashes and validation predictions, then score once. Exact development/test overlaps: zero.
17: For each of the 48,000 fitted images, exclude its own index and search the other 47,999 images. Three Euclidean neighbours, one vote each. A three-way tie goes to the lowest class ID, matching the classifier. 40,931 ÷ 48,000 = 85.27%. Validation: 85.38%. Test: 85.04%. These close scores give little evidence of a large generalisation gap.
18: Validation loss reached its minimum at epoch 12. Training stopped at epoch 17 and restored that checkpoint. Validation accuracy chose the wider CNN without weight decay. The original seed-42 checkpoint was already selected. Mean accuracy: 92.400% without weight decay and 92.339% with it. Mean shirt recall favoured weight decay: 78.94% vs. 75.81%. All runs used one split.
19: The frozen CNN’s Coat probability. One feature is a 14 × 14 quadrant. Absent quadrants come from the same reference image. Evaluate all 16 subsets of the four quadrants, averaging each over 20 training images (two per class). Average each region’s marginal change over possible orders. The baseline plus four signed contributions recovers each prediction. The beeswarm covers ten validation images per class. Other backgrounds or region boundaries can change the values; mixed images may look artificial.
